environments.name: Earth
environments.tagline: Buoyancy drives the classic flickering teardrop flame.

facts.label: Gravity
facts.value: 1 g (reference)

facts.label: Reference atmosphere
facts.value: Air: 21% O₂ / 79% N₂ at 14.7 psia (101.3 kPa)
facts.quote: normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

facts.label: Why flames are teardrops
facts.value: Hot gas rises, cool air is pulled in at the base
facts.quote: on Earth, hot gases from a flame rise and gravity pulls cooler, denser air to the bottom of a flame, creating the classic shape and flickering effect.

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

facts.label: NASA material screening
facts.value: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1: upward burning, pass/fail at 6 in (15 cm)
facts.quote: NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to assess flammability of materials ... Materials that do not self-extinguish after six inches of burning must undergo other special considerations

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

environments.data_note: 6 training rows at 1 g: the upward limiting-oxygen (ULOI / MOC) tests for Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex HT90-40 at NASA White Sands (NTRS 20130010991 Table I). No 1 g rows exist for the other materials, so the range guard refuses them in this tab.

environments.name: Moon
environments.tagline: Weak buoyancy: lunar gravity may be close to the MOST flammable condition.

facts.label: Gravity
facts.quote: For the Moon, the gravitational level is 1.62 m/s2, or 0.165 that of normal gravity.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Planned habitat atmosphere
facts.value: 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa), 34% O₂ / 66% N₂; control bands up to 37% O₂
facts.quote: HLS, Lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally use 8.2 psia / 34% O2, 66% N2 ... Control bands are expected to allow up to 37% O2

source.label: Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)

facts.label: Flammability at lunar g
facts.value: Near the most flammable gravity level
facts.quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

source.label: Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)

facts.label: Partial-gravity maximum
facts.value: Flammability peaks roughly between 0.15 and 0.4 g
facts.quote: the partial-gravity fire maxima occur roughly over the range bracketing the levels of concern for missions beyond Earth orbit, namely, 0.15 to 0.4 of normal gravity.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: First long-duration lunar-g burns
facts.value: LUCI: >25 s burns on a spinning New Shepard rocket
facts.quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.

source.label: Ferkul et al. (2025) Lunar Combustion Investigation (LUCI): Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket (NTRS 20250010653)

facts.label: Buoyant flow speed vs Earth
facts.note: Physics-based ESTIMATE: buoyant velocity scales as √(g·β·ΔT·L), so at fixed flame size and temperature it scales with √g. Not a measurement.

environments.data_note: 8 training rows at lunar g: ULOI*/MOC* for Mylar, Ultem, Nomex (drop-tower centrifuge, NTRS 20130010991) and 2 SIBAL downward-spread tests (parabolic flight, NTRS 20260001966; LUCI rocket, NTRS 20250010653). Low-g drop tests last only ~5 s.

environments.name: Mars
environments.tagline: Martian gravity: limits measured up to 5.75 points of O₂ below Earth's.

facts.label: Gravity
facts.quote: For Mars, this "partial gravity" level is 3.72 m/s2, or 0.380 that of normal gravity.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Habitat atmosphere
facts.value: Not yet baselined in our sources; NASA-considered exploration atmospheres include 10.2 psia / 26.5% O₂ and 8.2 psia / 34% O₂
facts.quote: NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.

source.label: NASA PSI-20 ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) investigation metadata

facts.label: Measured Martian-g limits
facts.value: Up to 5.75% O₂ lower than 1 g, typically between 1 g and lunar values
facts.quote: The limiting oxygen levels at Martian gravity were significantly lower than normal gravity (up to 5.75% O2 lower), and typically between the normal gravity and Lunar gravity values.

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

facts.label: Implication for screening
facts.value: 1 g tests may not be conservative
facts.quote: normal gravity material flammability screening tests may not be conservative and some materials tested to be safe for use in space may actually be flammable.

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

facts.label: Buoyant flow speed vs Earth
facts.note: Physics-based ESTIMATE from √g scaling of buoyant velocity. Not a measurement.

environments.data_note: 6 training rows at Martian g: ULOI*/MOC* for Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex HT90-40 (5.18 s drop-tower centrifuge, NTRS 20130010991 Table I). Every other material is refused in this tab.

environments.name: ISS
environments.tagline: No buoyancy: only ventilation and diffusion feed the flame.

facts.label: Gravity
facts.value: ~0 g (continuous free fall)

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

facts.label: Cabin atmosphere
facts.value: Air, 21% O₂ at 14.7 psia (101.3 kPa)
facts.quote: the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have operated at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

facts.label: Pre-EVA atmosphere
facts.value: 30% O₂ at 10.2 psia (70.3 kPa)
facts.quote: brief pre-EVA activities when oxygen levels are increased for a short period of time to 30% oxygen while the total pressure is lowered to 10.2 psia

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

facts.label: Flame shape
facts.value: Rounded or even spherical
facts.quote: In microgravity, this flow doesn't occur and on the space station, low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical.

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

facts.label: Role of ventilation
facts.value: Flames spread poorly in still air, vigorously in flows up to ~20 cm/s
facts.quote: Flames propagate poorly in truly quiescent conditions, but they are enhanced vigorously by low-rate atmospheric flows (velocities up to about 20 cm/s).

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Hard-to-see flames
facts.value: At very low airflow a flame can be pale violet and nearly invisible
facts.quote: At 1.0 cm/s, the entire flame is pale violet and nearly invisible

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Invisible cool flames
facts.value: FLEX found fuel still 'burning' after the visible flame went out
facts.quote: FLEX ... led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued “burning” under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

environments.data_note: 124 training rows in microgravity: NASA drop towers, Shuttle SSCE, ISS BASS/BASS-II (corroborated by the PSI-25 experimental table) and Saffire I-VI in Cygnus.

environments.name: Rocket transit
environments.tagline: Coasting to the Moon or Mars is free fall: the same physics as the ISS.

facts.label: Gravity while coasting
facts.value: ~0 g, identical to orbit
facts.quote: the environment in the transit phases of these journeys is microgravity, identical to the environment of Earth-orbiting spacecraft.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Why transit is harder
facts.value: Limited suppressant, delayed help from Earth
facts.quote: Stores of suppressant and atmospheric diluents are more limited ... and consultation and emergency communications with Earth controllers may be of poor quality and delayed.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

facts.label: Real spacecraft-cabin fires
facts.value: Saffire burned large samples inside uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft
facts.quote: Saffire is a series of experiments conducted aboard uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft after they depart the station

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

facts.label: Exploration atmospheres
facts.value: Reduced pressure with higher O₂ (e.g. 8.2 psia / 34%)
facts.quote: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.

source.label: NASA PSI-20 ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) investigation metadata

facts.label: Powered flight
facts.value: Most of the trip is unpowered; brief engine burns are not modelled
facts.quote: practical travel to the Moon or Mars must assume flight, for the most part, that is unpowered and without artificial gravity.
facts.note: During engine burns the crew feels thrust acceleration instead of free fall; no flame-spread data exist for that, so the tool models the coast phase only.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

environments.data_note: Uses the 124 microgravity rows; the Saffire (Cygnus spacecraft) rows are the closest real analogue to a crew-cabin fire in transit.

gas_mixes.label: Normal air (O₂/N₂)
gas_mixes.note: Every training experiment burned in O₂/N₂ (air or N₂-diluted / O₂-enriched air). Adjust O₂ and pressure with the sliders.

gas_mixes.label: Carbon dioxide build-up
gas_mixes.note: No flame-SPREAD experiment in the dataset used CO₂-diluted air, so the classifier refuses. Real related data: FLEX (PSI-69) burned fuel droplets in atmospheres with added CO₂; the table below summarises those real tests.

source.label: NASA PSI-69 FLEX investigation metadata + experimental table

gas_mixes.label: Methane leak
gas_mixes.note: No flame-spread experiment in the dataset had fuel gas mixed into the cabin air, so the classifier refuses. Related NASA work on methane flames: ACME BRE, SLICE and SPICE (gas-jet flames), cited below.

source.label: NASA Science - ACME mission page
